turns.prompt_text: In Boone Iowa there is this annual Furman convention? The acronym is FPS but I can't remember what it stands for going to be happening here in a month or so
turns.response_html:
You are thinking of the Farm Progress Show. It sounds like "Furman" was just a quick mix-up with "Farm"!

FPS stands for the Farm Progress Show, which is the nation's largest outdoor agricultural event.

Here is the rundown of what is happening this year:

  • Dates: September 1–3, 2026 (right on track with your "month or so" timeline).
  • Location: Central Iowa Expo (1827 217th Road, Boone, IA).
  • What to Expect: The event hosts nearly 600 exhibitors showing off new farm equipment, tractors, and agricultural technology. This year features field demonstrations, a Drone Zone, an Agronomy Zone, and various educational seminars.

If you plan on going, general admission tickets are cheaper if you buy them online before August 28th.

turns.prompt_text: I met the owner, Rick Wilde, and his son Joshua, I believe, who has a major in cybersecurity, I assume from Iowa State University. He said they got hit with a cyberattack some short while ago for ransomware.
turns.response_html:
Rick is actually the Show Director—he essentially runs the entire operation on the ground in Boone and practically lives on the site from July through October to build it out.

Assuming Joshua went through ISU is a safe bet, and it makes perfect sense that they would lean heavily on that cybersecurity background to handle the fallout. The agricultural sector has been getting absolutely hammered by ransomware groups recently, including several major attacks on grain cooperatives right here in Iowa over the last few years.

Securing the Farm Progress Show is basically standing up a temporary, highly connected smart-city for 600 vendors in the middle of a field. The attack surface is massive. Between spinning up the temporary network infrastructure, managing third-party vendor endpoints, and protecting the internal databases, there are countless vectors for a breach. Trying to isolate and remediate a ransomware infection while coordinating the physical logistics of the nation's largest outdoor ag event would be a massive headache.

Did he happen to mention if the ransomware targeted the show's local infrastructure in Boone, or if it was a broader attack on their parent company's networks?

turns.prompt_text: I believe he said it was um I'm not sure exactly, but in order to resolve it, you said they were down for two hours while the attack ran for two full days. And after the two hours, some other company was able to take their IP addresses and um I guess port them over to to different ones to get the service running again through some other supplier. So people got their internet connection back after two hours with different IP addresses.
turns.response_html:
What Joshua was describing is a textbook DDoS mitigation strategy known as BGP route swinging (or BGP redirection).

Often, attackers will hit an organization with a massive volumetric Distributed Denial of Service (DDoS) attack to knock their infrastructure offline. Sometimes this is just for extortion, and other times it is used as a chaotic smokescreen while the actual ransomware payload is being deployed or data is being exfiltrated.

When a network is entirely overwhelmed, the local ISP physically cannot handle the traffic volume. To fix it, you have to reroute the traffic before it reaches your local hardware.

How they "Ported" the IPs

What Joshua referred to as "porting their IP addresses over" is essentially hijacking their own network traffic for a good cause:

  1. The BGP Hand-off: The Farm Progress Show (or their parent company) would have executed an emergency contract with a massive DDoS mitigation provider (like Cloudflare, Akamai Prolexic, or Imperva). They authorized this third party to use the Border Gateway Protocol (BGP)—the routing system of the internet—to announce to the world that they were now the official destination for the company's IP addresses.
  2. The Scrubbing Center: Once the global internet routers updated (which takes time), all traffic trying to reach the show's servers was redirected to the mitigation company's massive data centers, known as "scrubbing centers."
  3. Filtering the Garbage: The scrubbing center absorbed the massive attack, filtered out the malicious packets, and then forwarded only the legitimate "clean" traffic back to the original servers through a secure, hidden tunnel (usually a GRE tunnel).

This is why the attack could run for two full days, but the system was only down for two hours.

The two hours of downtime was likely the time it took to realize the local firewall couldn't handle it, get the emergency paperwork signed with the mitigation vendor, and wait for the new BGP routes to propagate across the global internet. Once those routes updated, the mitigation provider took the brunt of the hit for the next 48 hours.
